claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite with discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite develops phase separation and interfacial voids under the relevant service conditions.
A thin Ti coating can be deposited on W surfaces before composite consolidation and heat treatment.
During heat treatment, the Ti coating reacts with residual or environmental carbon to form TiC.
The intervention produces a coherent, thin TiC interlayer at W/Cu interfaces.
The TiC interlayer acts as a diffusion barrier that limits W/Cu interdiffusion.
Limiting interdiffusion with the TiC interlayer suppresses phase separation.
The in situ TiC layer fills interfacial voids.
The TiC interlayer enhances bonding at W/Cu interfaces.
Improved interfacial bonding and fewer voids lower interfacial thermal resistance.
Ti-coated W–Cu composites will have fewer interfacial voids than untreated composites.
Ti-coated W–Cu composites will exhibit less phase separation than untreated composites.
Ti-coated W–Cu composites will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated composites under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
TiC can support improved performance under high heat flux and irradiation conditions relevant to plasma-facing applications.
The intervention is expected to remain effective within the temperature and irradiation-flux range relevant to fusion-reactor joints.
The intervention may lose effectiveness at temperatures or irradiation doses above those encountered in current fusion-joint designs.
The optimum Ti-layer thickness and the kinetics of TiC formation under irradiation are not established.
The effects of Ti or TiC on mechanical properties under cyclic loading remain insufficiently characterized.
